title: The mathematicians rebel against AI - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Responding to a statement on AI signed by Terry Tao and other math notables, Tyler Cowen argues the mathematicians' complaint is 'oddly early' and that their own adaptation, not the decisions of the companies controlling the technology, is the real action variable. He predicts funding for and interest in mathematics will rise considerably in the medium term, expects AI companies to 'act like companies', and accepts that human experts including himself are becoming subordinate to AIs.

insights.claim: Funding for mathematics and interest in the topic are expected to rise considerably in at least the medium term because AI makes math matter much more than it used to.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Contrarian to the 'AI displaces mathematicians' read — implies growing budgets and talent demand in math-adjacent research, not shrinking ones.
insights.quote: I expect the funding for mathematics, and the interest in the topic, to rise considerably, at least in the medium term.

insights.claim: The stakes on mathematics rise further if P vs NP goes 'the wrong way' or if the distribution of the primes turns out to be a little too predictable — outcomes that would bear directly on cryptographic security.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A low-probability, high-impact tail for anything resting on cryptographic hardness, including crypto assets and secure communications.

insights.claim: There is nothing stopping the mathematics community from awarding status, pay and promotions to people who fill in important blanks in mathematical understanding even when an AI has already proved or disproved the underlying theorems.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: The claim that whether AI benefits or destroys a field is determined by the decisions of the humans controlling the technology has no actual argument behind it; the main action variable is instead how well the affected professionals adapt to the new reality.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Reframes AI governance debates away from lab-control levers toward professional adaptation — bearish on the efficacy of guild-led restraint campaigns.
insights.quote: There is no actual argument for that proposition, and I would sooner expect that the main “action variable” is how well the mathematicians adapt to the new reality.

insights.claim: In the near future fewer economists will carry marginalist insights and modes of thought in their heads because the right answer can be obtained by pressing a button on an AI — a disturbing but expected erosion of internalized expert reasoning.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Human capital embedded in expert reasoning depreciates faster than credential-based models assume; relevant to valuing professional-services and education businesses.

insights.claim: Applying Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen distinction, the benefits to economic science from AI are expected to be enormous even though current practitioners cannot foresee most of those benefits today.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Structural argument for discounting practitioner surveys of AI's value — the upside is systematically invisible to incumbents.

insights.claim: Solving famous dramatic math problems is the current commercial priority of the major AI companies, but as the AI space grows, paths toward AI that produces, articulates and teaches mathematical understanding are likely, with human mathematicians best placed to lead them.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
